Will the hon. member permit a question. I am sure we are all interested in what he is saying. Perhaps I have two questions. First, when he says it would be a good idea to find some other way than the use of the strike by labour to enforce its wishes, has he any precise suggestion to make? Second, when he advocates that the minister get into

May 27. 1966
Supply-Labour
the negotiations at an earlier stage, is there not some fear that this could be interpreted as government interference in free, collective bargaining? I use the phrase "free collective bargaining" because it is something 1 value, but I will also use a term that appeals to him and refer to interference with free private enterprise.

I quite appreciate the hon. member's position. In answer to the first question as to what could be done to protect the workers' interests if the strike weapon were not used, I suggest there is another factor, namely, the general public interest, that is becoming far more important in these labour-management disputes. I suggest it is up to the parliament of Canada and the Minister of Labour as the administrator of the policies of this parliament to protect that public interest. Even though it may not be acceptable to management in some cases or labour unions in other cases, I feel we have probably reached a stage in our economic and social development where we are going to have to accept some form of arbitration by the federal government. In the first instance, of course, it would have to be authorized by the federal parliament and its elected representatives who are the spokesmen for the public interest.
I am not suggesting that this can be done at once. I am not going to suggest that I know all the answers. However, I am going to suggest that the public interest has been hurt a sufficient number of times in the past that we should have come to the point of realizing that perhaps some form of compulsory arbitration is going to be necessary in the future.
In so far as the other question is concerned and the hon. member's point about interference in free collective bargaining, may I say I did not suggest that the minister should start directing which way the negotiations should go, but it seems to me that all too often no mediator is appointed until several weeks after the strike. I can appreciate the difficulties involved here because we would hope that management and labour unions would get together and solve their problems without having the government move in.
The point I want to make is that even after a mediator is appointed it usually takes at least a few days, and in some cases several weeks, before he can familiarize himself with the positions taken by the labour union and management. No one can deny that this is a
fMr. Knowles.]
fact. I suggest that a great deal of this lost time could be saved if the Department of Labour would take an active interest and follow the negotiations right up to the point where they break down. Then there would not have to be a waiting period while the mediator familiarizes himself with both sides of the dispute. I do not know whether that answers my hon. friend's questions satisfactorily but in any event that is my answer.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I wonder whether it answers the hon. member's own question?

I think it does. In closing I simply want to say again that the public interest has been harmed by strikes so many times in the past I think we should recognize that something needs to be done. I believe the first step would be for the department or the minister to follow the negotiations more closely, having in mind some person to act as mediator immediately a strike is called. If we require new legislation to give effect to the suggestions I have made, we in this party are prepared to support the minister if he presents such legislation.

Mr. Chairman, in entering this debate for a few moments I should like to make some comments about the Atlantic economy and in particular about the degree of unemployment that exists there at the present time, has existed and will continue to exist unless the government takes some action other than that indicated to date in legislation and in the budget. It is small comfort for the people who reside in the Atlantic provinces to be told about the low level of unemployment in Canada. When there are no jobs to be had, when there are long line-ups of people looking for jobs in many areas of the Atlantic provinces, there is not much satisfaction to be gained from the fact that there is low unemployment in Ontario, British Columbia, the western provinces or wherever the minister desires to point.
This government has deserted the Atlantic provinces in so far as any proposals have been made that would be of benefit in a special way. The government has deserted the area, ignored it and endeavoured under one of its programs to move the people to other parts of Canada in the hope it will get rid of the problem.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Since it took office in 1963 it has not faced the fact that the situation in the Atlantic
May 27, 1966

provinces is different from that in the rest of Canada. It has not come forward and proposed the special kinds of programs suggested to it, the kind of programs which were adopted in the five years prior to 1963 when the Conservative administration held office. This is our great plea in endeavouring to make the government aware of the situation which exists. Apparently they are not aware of it or if they are they forget about it, ignore it and ask what difference it makes because the area is too small to worry about anyway.
I see that the Minister of Fisheries is now in the house. I often wonder what he does at cabinet meetings when proposals which have been made by various organizations in the Atlantic provinces to stimulate employment in the area are discussed. Let me take, for example, the designated area policy which excludes certain areas in the Atlantic provinces. Where was he when they were first considered in cabinet? Does he agree with the decision of the government? Does he agree with the policy that excludes Halifax, Dartmouth, Saint John and Fredericton? Does he think that leaving these areas out is good for employment in the Atlantic provinces? We never know.
Go back five or six years.
It would be much better for the Atlantic provinces if we did. At least we would get some attention from the government.
How blind can you be?

The great difficulty, Mr. Chairman, is that those from the Atlantic provinces in the Liberal cabinet all seem to be blind because they never seem to be able to convince their colleagues that anything which will specifically benefit the Atlantic provinces should be adopted by the government.
There are none so blind as those who will not see.

As my colleague from Carleton says, there are none so blind as those who will not see. Certainly the Minister of Fisheries has ignored the problems facing the Atlantic provinces, and there is no place where those problems are worse than in his own constituency.

I invite the hon. member to come and see for himself.
Supply-Labour

I thank the minister very much but I visit his area probably as often as he does. I suggest to the minister that he had better go there more often if he thinks things are not bad in his area. I should like to know what are the unemployment statistics for Gloucester and also for Restigouche-Madawaska. They are shocking, and he knows it as well as I do; there is no doubt about it. But he would like to brush the matter off and ignore it.
I did make mention of one program, Mr. Chairman, but I should also like to ask the Minister of Fisheries whether ne agrees with the action of the Minister of Finance in rescheduling, as he so calmly put it, the construction of the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway. Was the minister in the cabinet when the decision was made to set it back and perhaps forget about it?
Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he aware that tenders have been called for the second phase of the Northumberland causeway?

I am aware that they have been called, Mr. Chairman, but I am also quite sure they can be cancelled just as easily as the project could be rescheduled. I would ask the minister whether he was in agreement with the Minister of Finance in the rescheduling and setting back of the construction of the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway. This is a pretty important project for New Brunswick, and the minister is the representative of New Brunswick in the cabinet. I should like some idea of where he stood on the question. I should like some idea of where the Atlantic provinces ministers stand on these special programs which are presented to the cabinet but ignored time and time again by the government.
I should also like to know where the ministers from the Atlantic provinces were when the budget was prepared, a budget which completely ignored the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada that special fiscal policies should be applied to the Atlantic provinces in order that tight money would not do the irreparable damage now being wrought in our area of Canada.
We cannot find out from anyone in the house what is going to be done with the coal industry of Nova Scotia. Members of our party have asked questions of everyone who could possibly be asked on the government side concerning the Donald report, but no one

May 27, 1966
Supply-Labour
in the government seems to want to take responsibility for the report or for informing the house what recommendations have been made, if they have been placed before the government.
This, Mr. Chairman, is especially irritating to me because in the election campaign of November, 1965 I listened to the programs presented over radio and television by this government which was going to do wonderful things for the people of the Atlantic provinces. I listened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare tell the people of Nova Scotia how he arranged $25 million for the coal industry. You would think it was a blank cheque that we could have filled in for any amount, $25 million, $50 million or $100 million.
What happened to that $25 million?
The cheque bounced. It was a bad cheque.
What about your Atlantic Development Board fund?

The Minister of Fisheries asks about the Atlantic Development Board fund. Let him tell me what happened to the $20 million designated for the use of Nova Scotia and which the government did not give Nova Scotia for two years. When we were in office we set up the Atlantic Development Board and put all of the resources of the government of Canada at the disposal of the board for projects which would be of benefit to that area.
But what has happened now, Mr. Chairman? The fund is bankrupt. The $100 million has gone. The money has either been spent or committed. The Minister of Transport said we would get more but a perusal of the order paper reveals nothing to that effect. Let the minister tell me where there is any resolution on the order paper to provide an increase in the fund. A minister from the Atlantic provinces should know this.
The agricultural industry of Nova Scotia and the Atlantic provinces has been waiting for a resolution on feed grains to get off the order paper but it does not seem to move. We have been waiting three years for it but nothing has happened. The farmers of the Atlantic provinces still have the same problems they had the day this government took office, and they will continue to have them just as long as this government stays in office. There is no doubt in the minds of the people

in the Atlantic provinces with regard to this fact, and they indicated their feelings in no uncertain terms in the last election campaign. If there were another one tomorrow they would indicate their feelings even more strongly than the last time.
While this government is in office we in the Atlantic provinces are in the position of having no place to go but down. The government will not do anything for us. We were kicked around by the Liberals for 22 years from 1935 to 1957. The people were given the opportunity to do something for themselves after that time. They did not have to come hat in hand to the government as was the case when Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Mackenzie King were prime ministers of the country. They came forward with proposals which were recognized, and action was taken as a result which was beneficial to the people of the Atlantic provinces. Where are we now? We are right back where we were during the 22 years when the Liberals were in office before.
Today we have some fairly aggressive premiers in the Atlantic provinces. They have banded together and are endeavouring to do as much as they can for their provinces. Anything happening today in the Atlantic provinces is a credit to the premiers in that part of Canada and is no credit to the federal government which has done nothing but damage to our economy every time it has introduced a piece of legislation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
To give hon. members an indication that I am not alone in thinking this way let me quote from an article in the Fredericton Gleaner of Wednesday, March 30, 1966: The article deals with the budget in these words:
-we have once more the frustration thrust upon us of having a "boom-busting" budget applied to our area which lags grievously behind the rest of Canada by every measure of comparison.
The gap between the average income in Atlantic Canada and that in the rest of Canada is not closing. And in this area deflationary policies must be deadly in their adverse effect.
The setting back of the Prince Edward Island causeway is a case in point. It is a cynical act which belies the federal government's pretense that the Atlantic economy is to be raised by federal policy to a fair sharing with the rest of Canada.
Mr. Sharp has shown no realization that his "brake on the boom" measures are totally unrealistic when applied to the Atlantic provinces where unemployment stands at almost 11 per cent of the working force.

Eleven per cent?
May 27, 1966

Eleven per cent. We hear the Minister of Labour telling us about the wonderful figures respecting unemployment. No one will say that there is an 11 per cent average unemployment rate throughout Canada, but I am saying that the unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces is 11 per cent and a government worth its salt should do something to eliminate that.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he seriously suggesting that there is an unemployment rate of 11 per cent, or even anything like that, in the province of New Brunswick to which he specifically referred? Is he seriously suggesting that?
I am seriously suggesting that according to the last figures I saw the average unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces was 10.9 per cent of the labour force.
When was that?
March 11.
That was an average of 11 per cent?
Nearly.
What year was that?

In 1966. Is the minister indicating by his attitude that we have not much to complain about in the Atlantic provinces? Is the minister going to tell us that the unemployment rate is 2.4 per cent or 5 per cent? No, he is not, because he knows it is a great deal more than that. No government should accept an unemployment rate of over 5 per cent as a satisfactory state of affairs.
You accepted it in 1960 and 1961.

We did not accept it and we did all kinds of things about it. Unemployment in Canada is as low as it is because of actions taken when we were in office. In reading the writings of any economist or even reading the report of the Economic Council of Canada established by the Liberal government it will be seen that the present boom started in 1961. I will tell you what started the boom. It started at about the time we devalued the dollar. We were ridiculed and made fun of by the Liberal party, which today embraces that measure and says it is the most wonderful thing that ever happened. What did the former minister of finance, the present hon. member for Davenport, say
Supply-Labour
about it? He said: "It is great, wonderful". Yet he was the man who conceived the "Diefendollars". He told the people that their money was worth only 93 cents. He said: "It was the right thing to do but you did it the wrong way".
I am going to read to the Minister of Labour, since he is so concerned about the figures I am quoting, a statement from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council report. I shall read from the April issue. I am sure the minister will not argue with the figures given here even though he seems anxious to argue with my figures. I quote from page 5:
-the regional unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces averaged 7.5 per cent in 1965. This was more than twice the rate of 3.6 per cent for the other six provinces, and even higher than the national rate of 7 per cent during the 1960-61 recession years when the national economy was operating at 91 per cent of capacity. Last year the ratio of national output to the economy's potential was 97 per cent.
I say to the Minister of Labour and his cabinet colleagues, especially those from the Atlantic provinces, that the Atlantic provinces cannot afford to have every proposal we put forward to the federal government turned down and ignored, as has been done repeatedly since this government took office. The government must wake up and realize the special problems existing in the Atlantic provinces which it is the government's responsibility to cure. Realistic proposals have been made to the government. These should be looked into because they are of value and would benefit that part of the country.
One special project I should like to mention is the harnessing of the Bay of Fundy tides. The government has dragged its feet with respect to this proposal ever since it took office. By contrast, when I was in Tennessee last week I saw the tremendous job that the Tennessee Valley Authority had done on a project started under President Roosevelt. Harnessing the Bay of Fundy tides would provide power and do the same sort of thing for the Atlantic provinces that the United States project to which I have referred did for the state of Tennessee. If the Bay of Fundy project were endorsed and implemented with the speed one would expect from a government that should be as concerned as we are about the high unemployment rate and the lack of prosperity everywhere in evidence in the Atlantic provinces, many of our problems would be ameliorated. It is this sort of thing that the Minister of Labour will

May 27, 1966
Supply-Labour
have to take cognizance of if he is to do the job I am sure he wants to do.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that the Minister of Labour would prefer to wait until all the speeches are made before he answers individual questions. But I wonder if I could not persuade the committee to alter this slightly with respect to the question I put to the minister this morning on orders of the day. I should like to put that question to him again and perhaps the committee would permit him to answer it. After that perhaps I might be permitted to make the rest of my remarks, although they will be brief.
On orders of the day this morning I asked the minister whether he would consider offering to the parties in connection with the Air Canada dispute the services of a top-flight mediator. The minister replied to the effect that he had not yet received the report of the conciliation board. I confess that when he made that statement it took me somewhat aback because, like some other people, I was relying on what 1 had read in the press and I understood that the report had already been approved by management but rejected by the employees. It therefore seemed strange to hear the minister say he had not received it despite the references to it which have been made in the news in the last day or two.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
My question is one which perhaps I can repeat. In the hope that this dispute may not go right down to the wire, I wonder whether it is not possible for an early offer of a top-flight mediator to be made to the parties in order that this dispute may be settled at an early date. I would appreciate the minister answering that question. After he has done so I should then like to make a few more remarks.

In spite of the request I made to the committee earlier I would be pleased, with agreement, to deal with this particular question. It is not unusual when a board of conciliation has finished its deliberations for the representation members of the board, generally with the encouragement of the chairman, to try to work out a settlement along the lines of the report itself. Then they are able to report a settlement as a fait accompli.
I cannot say definitely in this case what the situation is. I made inquiries repeatedly yesterday in consequence of a question put to me by a member of the hon. member's own party. I made careful inquiries and found

that the report had been typed and signed by at least one of the conciliation board members. But it certainly had not reached my office when I entered this chamber today. Whether it has done so by now I do not know.
However, I can assure the hon. member that when this report comes to hand both the minister and the senior officials of the department will be very glad to consider the appointment of a mediator to tie up any loose ends and do anything constructive which may prevent such a strike, as has been suggested.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I thank the minister for making that reply. I am sure all of us hope that the steps which the minister is prepared to take will result in an early settlement of this dispute.
While I am on my feet may I express a few thoughts for the minister to mull over in his spare time between his handling of labour disputes, going to the I.L.O. conference in Geneva, and so on. First, I want to support the contention which has been made by others that every effort be made by the minister and his department to secure at the earliest possible date full implementation of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code as passed by parliament last session. It took us a long while to get this legislation on to our statute books. We hope it will not be too long before its provisions are fully implemented.
I would also urge the minister not to regard the implementation of the code in its present terms as the last word. He knows that when the bill was going through the house we urged that some of the minimums ought to be higher. I urge him even now to begin thinking of the desirability of raising the minimum wage rate from the $1.25 figure now in the code to a figure not less than $1.50. I remind him of the news report from Washington a few days ago that steps are to be taken by the present United States administration to raise the minimum wage in that country to $1.60 an hour. I support those who believe there should be parity of wage rates between our two countries. It seems to me that to ask for $1.50 as a minimum rate in Canada is little enough.
I would urge also that another look be taken at the length of vacations provided in the code. The minister spoke with some pride, not as a cabinet minister, I think, but as a Canadian, in the fact that we have made progress in the last few decades and that we now provide holidays for the workers of this
May 27, 1966



country to a far greater extent than we did a few decades ago. It appears to me that bearing in mind the tempo of modern living, the effects of automation and so on, we should begin to think in terms of the desirability of longer vacations than those we have yet provided by law.
It seems to me that the least the minister might do would be to steal a couple of bills which are on the order paper in my name. One asks that the minimum wage rate be raised to $1.50 and the other calls for a minimum paid holiday of three weeks after a few years of employment. This is one form of theft to which we do not object. I would even facilitate the minister taking over these bills. However, if he does not accept the offer we shall debate them one of these days during private members' hour.
I am glad to know that steps are at last being taken to deal with the proposal that Canada should have a labour safety code. It is an ironic touch, and I am not too happy about it, that a piece of labour legislation is being started in the other place. I shall not expand on that at the moment. We are just glad to get it.
There are many shops and factories in this country where because the type of employment comes under federal labour jurisdiction there is no right of the province to supervise health and safety standards. Many people suffer because of this situation. The need for supervision of health and safety standards in plants coming under federal jurisdiction is clear and I hope this legislation, when we get it, will meet the need.
Another area in which action has long been promised, certainly since the present Liberal government came to power, concerns the Unemployment Insurance Act. There are a good many spots in this legislation which need to be overhauled. We were promised a couple of years ago that this would be done soon-that is a standard phrase we get from the other side of the house. I hope the present minister, who has shown signs of wanting to get things done, will try to get some action with respect to improvements in this act.
I would remind the minister also, though perhaps he was referring to this earlier today, of his longstanding promise to do some basic research into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I believe his predecessor promised us a couple of years ago that he would get moving on this legislation, but we have not seen any signs of this yet. I
Supply-Labour
hope the hon. gentleman will get on with it soon.
I should also like to urge that there be some concrete action with respect to the recommendations of the Freedman commission. The minister today extolled Mr. Justice Freedman on the tremendous job he did in producing this report. I share in the accolade paid to Mr. Justice Freedman but I was rather disturbed when the minister, as I thought I heard him, said we might not have to deal with that report in this house. I cannot read all of the speeches that the minister makes to various bodies around the country because he and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State are sending us their speeches all the time and we just cannot keep up with them. But it seems to me I read in a speech which the minister delivered before a labour body not many days ago a suggestion that early action in the house on the Freedman commission report might be necessary.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In my view he was perfectly right in referring to the subject matter covered by that report as an important one, a key one for our times. Let us not wait 10, 20 or 30 years to deal with the problems outlined in the Freedman report. It took us that long to get some of the things which the Liberals promised in 1919-nearly half a century in some cases. Here is something that should be dealt with now.
The only other comment I would like to make relates to the exchange between the hon. member for Medicine Hat and me, when he was speaking on the question of what labour can do to win the things it seeks on the economic front. There is no doubt in my mind that people generally hold the opinion that strikes are unfortunate. It would be desirable if we could find some other way to deal with industrial disputes when they go down to the wire rather than by having strikes. But it seems to me that those who say we must find some other weapon face the obligation to tell us what that other weapon could be.
I do not like strikes any more than anyone else does, but neither do I want workers to be put in a position where they have to take what is handed to them without any means of expressing the rights we enjoy in a free society. I thought it was interesting that the hon. member for Medicine Hat, in his honest

May 27. 1966
Supply-Labour
effort to come up with some answer, could only suggest arbitration, indeed, compulsory arbitration. When one starts to talk about that I do not see how one can get away from the fact that this is interfering with the process of collective bargaining and all the procedures of freedom generally.
I am ready to go along with those who say let us find some better way, but until people have found a better way I do not think they have the right to suggest that the strike weapon should be outlawed. We shall return to this subject when we discuss the civil service collective bargaining bill because, in presenting that legislation, the government has to some extent recognized the right to strike in an area where it has not previously been recognized, and I shall have something to say about the matter when we discuss that bill.
I merely urge that when we talk about labour relations and ways of settling disputes between labour and management it should not be idle talk. It should be the kind of discussion that results in something specific, and in the absence of some other way let us not for a moment consider departing from ways that recognize the just freedoms we enjoy in our kind of society. These freedoms are enshrined in the right to organize and in the right to free collective bargaining and nothing should be done to abolish those rights. I am not criticizing the minister. I am just dealing with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
I thank the minister for his answer on the Air Canada situation and I hope that in his free time he will think pretty seriously about some of the things I have suggested to him.

Mr. Chairman, it is very interesting to me to take a look at what has happened in this country over the past several years and to see the changes that have taken place with regard to the labour situation in various parts of the country. I recall the years when the leader of my party was prime minister and unemployment was a problem, and I recall some of the actions taken at that time to try to meet the challenge of that situation. I refer particularly to the vocational training and vocational school building programs and to some of the results which have flowed from them.
Because of the training that has taken place and because of the promise of the South Saskatchewan River project, the province of Saskatchewan is experiencing a definite shortage of domestic help and farm

labour. This is significant at a time when the number of farms in the province is declining at a greater rate than ever before in our history.
I have here a letter which I received from a lady the day before yesterday in which she says she has been trying for five months to get domestic help to assist with her family and home. I got in touch with the national employment office in Ottawa and asked if people were available for this type of work. Their answer was that there are 175 applications for domestic help in the city of Ottawa that cannot be filled, and I imagine that situation is common in many areas across the country.
Canadian farmers are finding it almost impossible to secure the help they require, and I take this opportunity to urge the minister to use his good offices to impress upon the government the need of bringing greater numbers of people into Canada who would undertake this type of work.
Farm operators in Saskatchewan and other areas are looking for legislation that will allow people who have unemployment insurance books to take jobs on farms and secure stamps for such employment. This is a cautious, first step that could be embarked upon without any great danger of the abuses feared by those who have considered this problem in the past.
I would also like to stress to the minister the need for providing more training for the retarded, the blind and the disabled. It is interesting to note that item No. 45 on the order paper, the Canada Assistance Plan legislation, is to provide assistance in this direction. I would like the minister to tell us whether this means that the problem of training or retraining people in these categories is now going to become a responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare rather than of the Department of Labour.

The department of manpower possibly.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

It is being introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The other problem which exists in the province of Saskatchewan, and I believe also in other provinces, is a matter which was brought to the attention of the house some time ago by the hon. member for Saskatoon. It has to do with hospital help and not only
May 27, 1966

in respect of hospitals but also homes for senior citizens. There is a real need in this regard. I believe the government knows there also is a shortage of nurses and that programs to try to meet this problem are required. With the advent of a national health program such as apparently is envisaged by the government, this need will become more acute. I believe a great deal more attention should be given to this problem than has been given to it up to the present time.
In closing I should like to impress upon the minister how urgent I think it is that something should be done to bring some of the people who are engaged in farm labour under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I know this is not one of the easiest problems in the world to solve. There may be a fear that there will be some abuse, but certainly the farm labour situation in this country today is such that it merits the government giving consideration to the extension to farm workers of the same benefits extended to those employed in any other vocation.

Mr. Chairman, in expressing our good wishes and our hopes for success in respect of the minister's meeting later this afternoon, we cannot overlook the fact that a good deal of this national grief could have been avoided had the minister undertaken two or three weeks before the fact the efforts he now is proposing to make. These situations do not develop overnight. The influence of automation on working conditions is not a surprise occurrence. Half an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure and we believe that the proper dosage should have been administered a month ago. Having had 20 years experience in negotiations on behalf of management, I know that private enterprise takes a dim view of governmental intervention, but even the most dogged private enterpriser will agree that when national interests are involved the prestige which lies in the person of the Minister of Labour should be welcomed.
We regret that such preventative action was not taken and that such a sobering influence was not introduced in respect of this problem, because not only are the economic effects disastrous but once the strike has started the conditions involved in the settlement always are more onerous to both parties, and the public is called upon to suffer even longer. Therefore, we very gladly join with those who suggest that in cases which
Supply-Labour
have such national consequences the office of the Minister of Labour together with his personal services and the prestige of his office should be offered to the parties involved so that an investigation can be made, first of all, into the very nature of the difficulty and, second, into the general area of agreement and the evils involved in the problem so that proper measures can be taken before, so to speak, the pot boils over.
I was amazed to hear the minister say that we never have been so prosperous. We received the same message from the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. Canadians, apparently, never have had it so good. Canadians, however, really wonder what the ministers are talking about because practically every Canadian I know is broke, is looking for money and is having a difficult time making ends meet. Certainly the same can be said in respect of the older citizens and, in fact, about practically every class of society today. People are up against it. Any increase they may receive in hourly revenue through negotiation usually is eaten up even before the increase comes into effect.
I do not know where all the prosperity is because things are tough. In Montreal we dread the end of the Expo year and the great boost which has been given to the local economy because we have no idea what the government's intentions are in respect of the situation. Plans must be made so that the sudden surge of labour on the local market can be absorbed in a healthy manner. We see tight-money policies being exercised now just as they were in 1956. We know that among the general after-effects of such measures are such things as recession. We know that in 1957 and 1958 this was the follow-up of such policies. Naturally we fear we are going to have a repeat performance. We are very anxious to see definite measures taken now so that we will be in a position to face the music when the problem arises. Mortgage money is not available and interest rates are going to blow up any time now. If we call this prosperity, I really believe we are kidding ourselves. I think we should look very closely at the situation and set up the machinery now which will create the type of conditions that will help us face the music when the time arrives.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I heard someone say "carried". If I thought that were true I would refrain from giving an explanation of the bill. The purpose of the bill is very reasonable. It is to limit, licence and regulate the exportation of basic and primary resources. This bill is very moderate in that I am not suggesting that the exportation of our natural resources be prohibited, because that would be unrealistic, particularly in those areas where it is economically possible. It is in the interest of all Canadians to be assured that our natural resources be utilized to the greatest extent possible for the benefit of the largest number of Canadians.
Many permits and licences that have been granted in the past under some of our regulatory bodies, for instance, in respect of gas and oil, have not taken into consideration the primary interests of the Canadian public in that secondary industry could have been developed in Canada if the exportation had not been allowed. This fact was very evident in respect of a permit granted by the National Energy Board some years ago allowing the exportation of petroleum condensates. It is true that these are by-products of the petroleum industry, coming off at the heavy end of the processing, and that there was no use for these particular products here, but it is also a fact that if we had decided not to issue that permit many factories would have developed in Saskatchewan and Alberta to manufacture such products as dyes, medicine including aspirin, synthetics of all types, paints and other products which are not being manufactured in areas south of the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rinfret).]

prairie provinces, particularly in suburban areas of Chicago.
I am particularly interested in this matter because of the iron ore production in northern Ontario. For many years this area was protected by a decision of the province of Ontario to the effect that the export of pulp from Canada was prohibited in its raw state. Many people thought that this decision would result in an inability to develop the pulp and paper industry in northern Ontario. However, that has not been the case. There are many pulp and paper mills in northern Ontario and many towns have been built and maintained through this development. This would not be the case if the lumber companies had their way because this material would be exported to the United States. This development has been highly successful and brings substantial returns to the people in the areas where the resource is derived.
It is also true that we have not paid much attention to the development of perpetual yields from our forests surrounding pulp and paper mills. If we had paid enough attention we would probably have been able to extend these yields rather than curtail them in some areas. These curtailments were perhaps necessary because of the lack of sales in traditional markets and the difficulty of competing because of the necessity to use road transportation services rather than water transportation.
In northern Ontario there is developing a new industry in the mining field. Many of the communities in northern Ontario developed as a result of gold mining. It is easy to export gold as a finished product in ingot form because the process is simple, and extraction is not sufficient to warrant the shipping of concentrates. This is also true of silver mines.
When iron ore was discovered in northern Ontario a new problem developed, and it is a problem I think we must face. The companies that put money into the development of iron ore in northern Ontario now have a large operation in the Kirkland Lake area. This ore is being shipped by the subsidiary company to the parent company steel mill in Pittsburgh. Anyone who has had any experience with iron ore knows that the production of iron and steel ingots requires a large working force. As to the structure of exports . . ., the future list will probably be dominated by a number of important staples of the present day-pulp and paper, lumber, non-ferrous metals, and asbestos. The tariff should be re-examined, not with a view to increased protection, but in order to encourage further processing of certain raw materials in Canada, in part for domestic purposes, but primarily for export. In the case of aluminum, copper, lead, and zinc, we export ingots. And with fairly

He then said:
This would be directly to our disadvantage. Therefore, we should use every tool at our disposal, including a more vigorous application of customs' procedures, to counteract what has now become official American policy. I believe that if this bill is passed, the tariff board will have to make a decision every time one of our primary raw materials is exported.
I have already spoken of some of the commodities which I believe it is agreed will become our largest exports in the future. However, I think we should give some consideration to a number of other major exports which cannot be so readily assessed at the present time. We have been recently faced in northern Ontario with the thought of diverting water from the Arctic watershed through James bay and the connecting areas into southern Ontario so as to raise the water level of the great lakes and allow the expansion of industrial development in areas adjacent to the great lakes. According to what we heard in the discussion that took place yesterday, the development of secondary industries along this waterway has proved to be a disadvantage to Canada and an advantage to the United States.
I think that before we start any diversion or export of water or any extension in the sale of gas and oil, we should first consider the interests of Canada. We are immediately faced with the problem that we have already engaged in long-term projects such as the Columbia river development by which we have diverted a large amount of our water resource to the United States without retaining any control over waters which will be necessary to Canada in the future. I am well aware of the fact that we had to ensure the operation of United States companies for a period of years, but I think that our primary responsibility is not to United States industry but to the Canadian public, and we should develop secondary industries in those areas in which this resource exists. I therefore think that our exports should not be in the field of

I know that the government is giving consideration to these matters, as are all Canadians. I think we have gone beyond the stage of being a colony of Great Britain, not because we terminated our relationship with Great Britain voluntarily but because of the changing economy and because the economic markets of Canada no longer lie in western Europe but in the United States. I think the day has now arrived when we should assess the situation in terms of the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations to enable Canada to negotiate the trading of manufactured goods rather than raw materials. I believe that this is the responsibility of all the members of the government and that all civic-minded persons in Canada should have this uppermost in their minds every time a long-term arrangement is made resulting in a loss of our resources which could be used for the development of Canada. I believe we should no longer consider ourselves as hewers of wood and drawers of water but should consider ourselves fortunate in the possession of the resources we have and be prepared to develop them to the utmost.
As I have said, this is a very moderate bill.
I do not say we should cease to export raw materials. What I say is that the tariff board should license all exports of raw materials at the appropriate time and according to the needs of our nation.
In closing I would like to remind hon. members that members on the other side are also concerned about this matter. I was quite impressed with what was said by the member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner) in the discussion that took place in the last few days. He was very concerned about the fact that copper supplies are more easily obtained by the Westinghouse Company from other countries than from Canada. They find great difficulty not only in meeting the price of copper, which is obviously an economic consideration for any secondary manufacturer, but also in obtaining supplies. They have found that it is difficult for them to obtain a reasonable supply of the copper which is being produced in Canada and exported. Of course, as the hon. member for Davenport has pointed out, this hinges on the subsidiary position of most of the companies in Canada and it applies as much to Westinghouse as to most other companies.
Let us not belittle the problem in relation to those areas where we have not exercised


in the past any restrictions on the development and exploitation of our national resources by subsidiary companies totally owned and operated by foreign countries. For example, take the case of Jones and Laugh-lin's Adams Mine in Kirkland Lake. It will be very difficult to say, now that they have built their plant and started their operation of feeding the steel mills in Pittsburgh, that we are going to take over and operate a steel mill in Canada. I agree that this would cause a considerable problem which would parallel the situation of Cuba in relation to the United States. Cuba said, "We will buy your plant and give you long-term bonds". The United States replied that they were not interested in this, that what they really wanted was to continue operating their subsidiaries in Cuba. Canada, which is much more polite and less hot-blooded than those banana republics, would approach this problem in a different manner.
I think we are going to have to face the problem with a view to the future. Sooner or later we will find ourselves in the position of supplying all our raw materials to the United States and buying them back in the form of manufactured products. If this were to happen, Mr. Speaker, it might be better for us to join the United States and undertake our own secondary development on a continental basis rather than a regional one.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this bill will get support from the government. I know that we cannot hope for anything but having it talked out. For this reason I hope that those who participate will give sympathetic consideration to some of the problems we have tried to raise. I hope that those who are similarly inclined to the hon. member for Davenport will give consideration to these problems along the lines of his assessment of Canada's economic future.

Mr. Speaker, as I read this bill and consider the remarks made by the hon. member who introduced it, I find little I can approve. I support the argument of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) and the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) when they talk about the need to expand secondary industry in Canada. There is no question about that. But that is not what the bill says. The bill asks us to impose restrictions on the export of raw materials and natural resources from Canada.
Rightly so.

I believe it is a completely false assumption to think it is possible to promote secondary industry by restricting primary industry. The history of economic development in the United States, in Canada and in all the other industrial areas of the world has followed a consistent pattern. Primary industry is developed first and secondary industry follows. There is no argument at all about the need to promote secondary industry in Canada not only for the benefit of our domestic markets but for export as well. But I am certain this cannot be achieved by closing our doors against the export of certain raw materials. There is already severe restriction on exports in these areas.
It is not so long ago that some people were telling us that if the export of natural gas from Alberta were allowed dire consequences for Canada would inevitably follow. As events turned out the prediction could scarcely have been less correct. Not only has there been an increase in the prosperity of the whole industry but the reserves in that particular oil field have doubled, even quadrupled.
